Old_Answer: Yes, they would have survived. The Lennon-McCartney credit was the most famous in the world and their collaboration proved to be the most successful of all songwriting teams. As far as the actual contribution by the other, it really depended on each song. With the White Album Lennon and McCartney seemed to have general disregard for each other’s songs and they did most of the overdubbing on their own songs. The majority of the songs on the White Album were written by one of them with minimal or even no input from the other. There even were songs on the White Album that were solely recorded by either Lennon or McCartney. Lennon was the only one to perform on the recording of his “Julia.” McCartney was the only one to perform on the recordings of his “Blackbird” and “Wild Honey Pie.” McCartney was the only Beatle to perform on some of his other songs, although the songs had orchestration by George Martin—”Martha My Dear” and “Mother Nature’s Son.” “Birthday” was definitely a 50/50 Lennon/McCartney collaboration. And I believe that Lennon contributed some lyrics to “Rocky Raccoon.” “Helter Skelter” may have had some contributions by Lennon. But “Revolution 9” was a collaboration between Lennon, George Harrison and Yoko Ono. Ono also contributed to “Bungalow Bill.” Lennon, I think, was the sole writer of “Good Night,” sung by Ringo. I wasn’t there, so I don’t know for sure. But I would guess that the other songs credited to Lennon and McCartney on the White Album could have been solely credited to the principal writer and lead vocalist. The Lennon/McCartney songwriting partnership was unlike the typical songwriting partnerships that came before. Those partnerships comprised a composer and a lyricist, such as George and Ira Gershwin, Richard Rodgers with Larry Hart, Richard Rodgers with Oscar Hammerstein, Carole King and Gerry Goffin, etc. Lennon and McCartney both wrote music and lyrics. Early on they’d write “eyeball to eyeball.” But later in their partnership either of them would write most of a song, often with minimal input from the other and sometimes with no input at all from the other.
